# Why this choice

A small Why? control beside a choice an agent made. On demand, it names the deciding factors and the options that lost, then offers Change this or Keep it.

Kind: component · Group: AI and agents · Status: built, import from @twoux/ui

## When to use

- When an agent picked between options for the person: a time, a supplier, a template, a route, a recipient list.
- When a requirement could not be met and the person should know.
- When the choice is easy to change and people may want to change it after seeing why.

## When not to use

- By default, on every output. Explanations on demand keep the screen quiet; use the origin label (ai-origin-label) to say where something came from.
- Sources for a claim. Use Citations and sources (citations-sources).
- Risks or doubt about the output. Use a Confidence note (confidence-note).

## Structure

1. Why? link beside the choice
2. Popover ("Why <choice>", deciding factors)
3. Not chosen (each option and why it lost)
4. Couldn't meet (a requirement that was dropped, if any)
5. Footer (Change this, Keep it)

## Guidelines

- Show the reasoning on demand, from a Why? link. Do not show it by default.
- Name the deciding factors in plain language, with the most important first.
- Name the options that lost and why, so the person can see the alternatives were considered.
- Say if a requirement could not be met ("Couldn't meet: no room free before 10:00"), not only what was satisfied.
- End with Change this and Keep it, so the explanation leads to control.
- Store the reasoning with the choice when it is made. Do not rebuild it later, or the explanation can drift from what actually happened.

## Content

- Title the popover "Why <the choice>": "Why Thursday at 14:00".
- Write each factor as a fact the person could check: "Everyone invited is free", not "Best fit".
- Write each lost option as its name, then the reason: "Wednesday 10:00: Imogen is out until 11:00".
- Keep buttons as verbs: "Change this" opens the choice for editing; "Keep it" closes the popover.

## Accessibility

- The control is a button with the hidden text "Why <choice>", so it is not just "Why?" out of context (SC 2.4.6, 4.1.2).
- The popover is a non-modal dialog opened by the button; Escape closes it and focus returns to the button (APG dialog).
- Deciding factors use a check icon and text, and the icon is hidden from assistive technology (SC 1.4.1).
- The target is padded to at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels (SC 2.5.8).

## Keyboard

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| Enter / Space | Open the Why? popover |
| Tab | Move through Change this and Keep it |
| Esc | Close the popover and return focus to Why? |

## Examples

### why

```tsx
import { WhyChoice, toast } from "@twoux/ui";

export const meta = { title: "Why the agent picked this", description: "A Why? link beside the choice. On demand it names the factors, the options that lost and what could not be met, then offers Change this or Keep it.", order: 1 };

export default function Example() {
	return (
		<div className="flex w-full max-w-xl items-center gap-2 rounded-sm border border-line bg-surface px-3 py-2.5 text-base text-ink">
			<span className="min-w-0 flex-1">Interview scheduled for <span className="font-medium">Thursday 14:00</span></span>
			<WhyChoice
				choice="Thursday at 14:00"
				factors={["Everyone invited is free", "It is inside the applicant's availability window", "Room 2 is booked for the full hour"]}
				alternatives={[
					{ name: "Wednesday 10:00", why: "Imogen Hart is out until 11:00" },
					{ name: "Friday 09:30", why: "Falls after the applicant's deadline to reply" },
				]}
				dropped="No slot was free before 12:00, which you asked for."
				onChange={() => toast("Opened the schedule for editing")}
				onKeep={() => toast("Kept Thursday at 14:00")}
			/>
		</div>
	);
}
```

## Related

- Citations and sources
- Confidence note
- AI origin label
- Agent run timeline
- Change review

# Filtering and search

Narrow a list to the rows that matter with filter pills that apply as you tick, show counts, and live in the URL.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** Hiring teams work through hundreds of listings and candidates and need to narrow them quickly. If every screen filters differently, people relearn the controls each time and links to a filtered list break.

**Solution:** Use the filter bar (pills) for list pages and the filter panel only for search across many fields. List values apply on tick with match counts, typed values apply on Enter, and the whole query is stored in the URL.

**Built from:** Filter pills and filter bar, Filter panel, List table, Data grid, Pagination and counts, Empty state, Saved views

## How it works

1. Show one or two of the most used fields as dashed pills next to Filter (F). Everything else sits behind Filter in a type-ahead list grouped into most used and all fields.
2. Opening a pill shows its values with the number of rows each one matches. Ticking a list value applies it at once; numbers and dates apply on Enter.
3. An applied filter becomes a solid pill that reads as a sentence: field, operator, value, for example "Status is any of Live, Expiring". Its remove button sits on the left.
4. Clear and the result count sit straight after the pills, so the person sees what is applied and how many rows match without opening anything.
5. Every change to a filter updates the URL, so reload, back and a shared link all reproduce the same list.
6. If nothing matches, the table is replaced by a zero results state with Clear filters as the action.

## When to use

- On any list page with more than one screen of rows: listings, candidates, pipeline, inbox.
- When people mostly narrow by two or three known fields such as status, location or team.
- Use the filter panel instead of pills when there are many fields to filter by, as in candidate search, and the panel can stay open beside the results.

## When not to use

- To find one known record by name or ID. Use search in the command palette (⌘K) or the view's search (/) instead.
- For view settings that always have a value, such as a chart's date range or Daily vs Weekly. Pills are removable, so these use a rectangle (segmented control or dropdown) instead.
- When several tables share one page. Filters in the URL become ambiguous, so filter each table locally and do not persist.

## Guidelines

- Filters act on the whole collection, not just the rows loaded on screen. The count says so: "Showing 5 of 412 candidates".
- Apply on tick because TwoUX's queries return fast; filter interactively when results come back almost instantly and in a batch when they are slow.
- If a query will take more than about a second, dim the results and show a progress indicator rather than redrawing after every tick.
- Show match counts on every list option so people avoid combinations that return nothing.
- Never put a filter row inside each column header. The pill bar keeps the whole query in one visible, shareable place.
- Validate filter values read from the URL and fall back to defaults when they are invalid. Never put personal data in the URL.
- Offer a plain search box alone when people know the exact name, such as a candidate's surname. Add pills when they choose among known values, such as stage or location.
- Show and/or wording only once two or more filters are applied; one filter reads as a plain sentence.
- Returning to a list by Back, the breadcrumb or the sidebar restores the filters the person left with.
- When a page has two filterable lists, only the main one writes its filters to the URL; the other keeps its filters on screen only.

## Content

- Pill text follows field, operator, value in sentence case: "Posted is in the last 30 days".
- Zero results heading: "No listings match these filters", then one sentence suggesting the likeliest fix, then a Clear filters button.
- Counts use the noun of the list: "14 listings", not "14 results".

## Accessibility

- Announce the new result count in a polite live region after each change, without moving focus.
- Each pill's remove button is its own Tab stop, named after its filter: "Remove Status filter".
- The value list is a combobox with a listbox: arrow keys move, Space ticks, Enter applies a typed value, Esc closes and returns focus to the pill.
- F to open Filter is a single-key shortcut, so it can be turned off in the shortcut sheet.

## Do

- Do keep the active query visible as pills at all times.
- Do show how many rows each value matches.
- Do write filters to the URL on every change.

## Don't

- Don't hide applied filters behind a single "3 filters" badge on desktop.
- Don't add an Apply button to a fast list filter; it adds a step for nothing.
- Don't use the empty state illustration and copy for a failed load. That is an error state.

## Related

- Saved views
- Selection and bulk actions
- Empty, loading and error states
- Keyboard-first navigation
- Filter pills and filter bar
- Filter panel


---

# Saved views

Store a filtered, sorted, column-chosen list under a name so people and teams return to it in one click.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** People rebuild the same filters every morning, and teams share screenshots of lists instead of links. Without one way to save, each screen invents its own favourites.

**Solution:** When filters are on, Save view stores filters, sort and columns together with a name. Views show live counts, mark unsaved changes, and reproduce from the URL.

**Built from:** Saved views, Filter pills and filter bar, Columns menu, List table, Data grid, Tabs (underline)

## How it works

1. Save view appears only once at least one filter, sort or column change differs from the default.
2. Save view asks for a name (required) and an optional description, validating duplicate names inline.
3. The view appears as a tab or sidebar item with its live row count, for example "Live 14".
4. If the person changes a saved view, its name shows an unsaved mark and the menu offers Update view, Save as new and Revert.
5. The view's state also lives in the URL, so a copied link opens the same view for anyone with access.

## When to use

- For lists people check repeatedly with the same filters, such as "My live listings" or "Closing this week".
- To give a team a shared starting point that everyone sees the same way.

## When not to use

- For a one-off filter. The URL already makes it shareable; use Filtering and search.
- For per-person display choices such as row density or wrapping. Those belong in the Columns menu and are remembered automatically.

## Guidelines

- A view stores filters, sort order, visible columns and grouping. Opening it restores all four.
- A default view loads when the page opens, unless the URL already carries filters.
- Changing a saved view never overwrites it silently. Updating needs an explicit Update view.
- Deleting a view uses a simple confirmation, because a team view can be in other people's sidebars.
- Keep the number of pinned views short; long rows of tabs slow the choice down.
- Group the views list into Team views and My views, and add a search box once there are more than about ten.
- People can set any view as their own default with Set as default. It is unavailable while the current view has unsaved changes, and the reason is shown.
- Update view shows the filters before and after in the menu, then saves with Undo in the toast.
- People can drop unsaved changes in any of three ways: Revert, choosing the view again, or Clear filters.

## Content

- Name views by what they contain, not who made them: "Closing this week", not "Rahul's view".
- Menu actions: "Save view", "Save as new view", "Update view", "Revert changes", "Delete view".

## Accessibility

- The unsaved mark is text ("Edited") as well as a dot, so it does not rely on colour.
- Confirm a save with a status message announced politely, not a moved focus.

## Do

- Do show the live count on each view.
- Do mark a modified view and offer Revert.

## Don't

- Don't save a view automatically when filters change.
- Don't store a view only in local storage; it must reproduce from its link.

## Related

- Filtering and search
- Keyboard-first navigation
- Saved views
- Columns menu


---

# Selection and bulk actions

Pick rows with X or checkboxes, then act on all of them from one bar above the table that says how many rows it will touch.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** Extending, closing or exporting listings one by one is slow, and bulk actions placed in different spots on each page are missed or misfired.

**Solution:** Selecting rows shows the bulk action bar directly above the table, with the actions, the count and Esc to clear. Filters and column headers stay where they were.

**Built from:** List table, Data grid, Bulk action bar, Checkbox, Toast, Confirmation dialog, Keyboard shortcut hint

## How it works

1. Select a row with its checkbox or X; ⇧J extends the selection downward. The header checkbox selects only the rows on the current page.
2. The bulk action bar appears directly above the table: the actions with their shortcuts on the left, the count ("2 listings selected") and Clear selection (Esc) on the right.
3. If more rows match than are on screen, the bar offers "Select all 412", and the count updates to say so.
4. Choosing an action runs it on the selected rows. Reversible actions show a toast with Undo; irreversible ones confirm first.
5. If an action cannot apply to some selected rows, say how many and why before it runs.

## When to use

- When the same action is often applied to many rows: extend, close, assign, export, ask the assistant.

## When not to use

- For an action on one record. Use the row's actions or the side panel.
- When the action needs per-row input, such as different closing dates. Use inline editing in the data grid.

## Guidelines

- Every bulk action is also available on a single selected row. The bar only adds the multi-row case.
- Labels are verb plus noun and say how many rows: "Close 2 listings".
- Keep the filters visible while rows are selected; the bar sits between the filters and the table instead of replacing the toolbar.
- Changing filters or sort clears the selection, so an action never touches rows the person can no longer see.
- Bulk results confirm in one toast ("2 listings extended") with Undo, not one toast per row.
- A bulk action that can't apply to the current selection stays in the bar as unavailable, with a reason: "Available when all selected listings are Live".
- The bar holds every action that can run on more than one record; row menus never offer "Close all" or similar.
- Order bar actions the same way as the page header: status actions first, destructive near the end, the main action last.
- Beyond four actions, the rest go in a More menu in the bar.

## Content

- Count format: "2 listings selected" in the bar, "2 of 24 selected" in the table footer.
- Destructive bulk confirmations name the count and the consequence: "Close 2 listings? They stop taking applications now."

## Accessibility

- Selected rows set aria-selected="true"; the selection is also shown with a tick, not colour alone.
- Announce the selection count when it changes.
- The header checkbox shows an indeterminate state when some rows are selected.
- Unavailable bulk actions use aria-disabled so their reason can be reached by keyboard.

## Do

- Do keep the count in the bar beside Clear selection, and name it in the toolbar's label so screen readers hear it before the actions.
- Do offer Undo after a reversible bulk action.

## Don't

- Don't replace the filter bar with the bulk bar; people lose sight of what they selected from.
- Don't silently skip rows an action can't apply to.

## Related

- Undo and destructive actions
- Keyboard-first navigation
- Data export
- Ask about what's on screen
- Bulk action bar


---

# Inline editing and validation

Edit values where they are shown, check each field when the person leaves it, and summarise every problem on submit.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** Errors that appear while typing feel like nagging, and errors that only appear after submit are hard to find. Each form in a product tends to validate at a different moment.

**Solution:** Validate a field when the person leaves it. In the data grid, Enter edits, Enter saves and Esc cancels, and invalid values stay in edit. On submit, a summary counts the problems and moves focus to the first.

**Built from:** Data grid, Text input, Form validation, Banner (inline alert), Side panel (drawer), Toast

## How it works

1. Show which values are editable: an edit affordance on hover in the side panel, cell focus in the data grid.
2. Enter starts editing; Enter saves and Esc cancels.
3. Check the value when the person leaves the field, never on the first keystroke.
4. If invalid, keep the cell or field in edit with a red outline, an icon and a message under it that says how to fix it.
5. Once the person is fixing an error, re-check on each keystroke so the message clears as soon as the value is valid.
6. On submit of a longer form, show a summary at the top that counts the problems and links to each, and move focus to the first field in error.

## When to use

- For values people change often, one at a time, such as a listing's closing date or owner.
- Across many rows in the data grid, where the same property is edited on many records.

## When not to use

- For creating a record or changing several dependent fields at once. Use a form in the side panel or a full page.
- In the list table. Only the data grid supports cell editing.

## Guidelines

- Read and edit states use the same type size and weight so text does not jump.
- In a filtered or sorted table, keep an edited row in place until the person refreshes, so it does not vanish under their cursor.
- Keep the submit button enabled on longer forms; pressing it runs validation and shows the summary.
- Mark required fields. If most fields are required, mark the optional ones instead.
- Server errors that belong to a field appear on that field; errors that belong to no field appear in a banner above the form actions.
- The error summary is in addition to field messages, never instead of them.
- Show requirements before anyone gets them wrong: constraint text under the field ("3 to 80 characters") and a format example. An error should never be the first time people see a rule.
- Warnings are not errors: a field warning ("Salary is below the range for similar roles") is shown in amber text and does not block saving.
- After submit, stay on the form until the server answers, with a spinner in the Save button. Never redirect first and lose the input.
- If a slow submit must leave the page, the result message links back to the form with the values and errors restored.
- A server error that belongs to a field, such as "A listing with this reference already exists", goes on that field, not in the banner.

## Content

- Required message: "[Field] is required", for example "Closing date is required".
- Say what is wrong and how to fix it in one sentence: "Salary must be a number, like 32000".
- Summary heading: "2 problems to fix", each a link to its field.
- Format errors start with Enter: "Enter a valid email address, like name@example.co.uk".
- Length errors give the count: "Job title has too many characters. 92 of 80." Counters read "Character count: 12/80".
- Don't use a generic top message such as "Fix the errors on this page"; the summary lists each problem.

## Accessibility

- Errors are text, not just a red border; colour is a second cue.
- Link each message to its field with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid on the field.
- On submit, move focus to the first field in error.
- In the grid, Enter or F2 enters edit, Esc restores grid navigation and may undo the edit.
- Placeholders are examples only; labels and constraint text carry the instructions, because placeholder text disappears and often fails contrast.

## Do

- Do validate on blur and clear the error as soon as it is fixed.
- Do keep save and cancel visible while editing.

## Don't

- Don't show errors on fields the person hasn't reached yet.
- Don't rely on a top summary alone.
- Don't report a failed save in a toast; keep the field in error with Retry.

## Related

- Empty, loading and error states
- Undo and destructive actions
- Record detail: side panel, overlay or full page
- Form validation
- Data grid


---

# Empty, loading and error states

One rule set for the three states every view has before or instead of data: loading, nothing to show, and failed.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** A blank table can mean loading, no data, no matches or a failure. When screens handle these differently, people wait for data that never comes or give up on data that was about to arrive.

**Solution:** Skeleton rows while loading, an empty state with one next step when there is nothing, a zero results state when filters match nothing, and an error state that keeps the filters and offers Try again.

**Built from:** Loading skeleton, Empty state, Error state (failed to load), Banner (inline alert), List table, Data grid

## How it works

1. Under about one second, show nothing extra. Beyond that, keep the table's shape with skeleton rows.
2. If the load succeeds with no records, replace the table with an empty state: what goes here, and one action to add it.
3. If records exist but filters match none, show the zero results state with Clear filters.
4. If the load fails, replace the table with an error state that says what failed, keeps the filters and offers Try again (R).
5. When a refresh fails after data has loaded, keep the old data on screen and show a warning beside the refresh time.

## When to use

- On every table, grid, chart card, panel and assistant answer that loads data.

## When not to use

- For a brand new workspace with nothing set up. Use Onboarding to an empty workspace with the setup checklist.

## Guidelines

- Never show "No listings" before loading has finished; people stop waiting and miss the data.
- Skeletons for structured content (tables, cards); a spinner for a single element such as a button or expanding row; a progress bar beyond about ten seconds.
- Empty and zero results states replace the table and its headers, so screen readers don't meet an empty table.
- Every state offers a next step. No dead ends.
- Errors never use the empty state component; they use the error state or a banner.
- Show when data was last updated after each refresh.
- Charts follow the same states with chart-specific shapes: the plot skeleton while loading, an empty state for no data, a no match state with Clear filters after filtering, and an error state with Try again, each inside the chart card so the title and controls stay.
- Manual refresh lives in the table header as an icon button labelled "Refresh listings", next to "Last updated 2 minutes ago". Add a refresh button only where data changes while people watch; other views refresh on load.
- During a refresh keep the current rows on screen and usable; only the refresh button shows a spinner.
- If a refresh takes longer than about ten seconds, show a "Taking longer than usual" status beside the refresh time; if it partly fails, show a warning status there with what failed and Try again.
- Wrap each region (table, chart card, side panel) in its own error boundary, so a crash shows an error state in that region and the rest of the page still works.
- Inside a table or read-only details, an empty value shows a muted hyphen (-) with the accessible name "Not set". Never use a dash for a real zero; show 0.
- Keep the count in the table heading even when empty: "Listings (0)".

## Content

- Empty: "No listings yet" plus "Create listing". Zero results: "No listings match these filters" plus "Clear filters".
- Error: "Couldn't load listings", then the likeliest cause, then "Your filters are kept." Avoid "sorry" and error codes.
- Loading text names the thing without articles or end punctuation: "Loading listings".
- The empty state's action uses the same label as the header button it mirrors ("Create listing") and is a secondary button, since the header already has the primary.
- An empty state description explains why it is empty and never repeats the heading or button text.

## Accessibility

- Announce loading, loaded counts and failures as status messages without moving focus.
- Hide decorative empty state illustrations from screen readers with empty alt text.
- Error states are identified in text, not only with a red icon.
- The refresh button has loading text ("Refreshing listings"), and the new "Last updated" time is announced politely.

## Do

- Do keep the layout stable from skeleton to data.
- Do keep filters when a load fails.

## Don't

- Don't use a full-page spinner for a table load.
- Don't show a frame-only skeleton with no placeholder rows.
- Don't write jokes into error messages.

## Related

- Filtering and search
- Onboarding to an empty workspace
- Generated table columns and enrichment
- Empty state
- Loading skeleton
- Error state (failed to load)


---

# Undo and destructive actions

Decide between Undo after the fact and a confirmation before it, using one test: can the action be reversed, and who else does it reach?

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** Confirming everything trains people to click Yes without reading; confirming nothing loses data. Teams pick differently on every screen.

**Solution:** Reversible actions run at once and offer Undo in a toast and with ⌘Z. Irreversible actions, or ones that reach people outside the workspace, confirm in a dialog that states the consequence, with the safe option focused.

**Built from:** Toast, Confirmation dialog, Bulk action bar, Button, Keyboard shortcut hint

## How it works

1. Ask: can TwoUX reverse this fully? Extending, renaming, archiving and moving can be reversed; deleting, emailing candidates and closing a listing that has notified applicants cannot.
2. Reversible: run it, then show a toast such as "2 listings extended" with Undo. ⌘Z undoes the last action too.
3. Irreversible: open a confirmation dialog titled with the action and count, stating what happens and what is kept.
4. Buttons name the outcome: the safe option ("Keep open") and the action ("Close listings"). Focus starts on the safe option.
5. For severe actions that also remove related records, such as deleting a workspace, ask the person to type the name.

## When to use

- Undo: for every reversible change made by a person or applied by the assistant.
- Dialog: for deletion, sending to people outside the workspace, and actions that cascade.

## When not to use

- Don't confirm routine reversible actions; offer Undo instead.
- Don't use a toast as the only record of something important; important outcomes also appear in the record's activity.

## Guidelines

- Scale friction to severity: none for low-risk, one dialog for high-risk, typed confirmation only for the rarest, most damaging actions.
- The dialog body names the items, the consequence and what stays: "The 140 people who already applied stay in your pipeline."
- Undo stays reachable after the toast goes: ⌘Z and the record's activity both reverse the last action.
- An Undo toast stays while hovered or focused and does not close while the person is reading it.
- The action button uses the danger style and sits to the right of the safe option, never on its own.

## Content

- Dialog title is a question with the count: "Close 2 listings?"
- Never "Are you sure?", "Yes" or "OK". Use outcome labels.
- Toast: past tense plus Undo: "Listing archived. Undo".

## Accessibility

- Confirmation dialogs use role alertdialog with aria-labelledby and aria-describedby.
- Focus moves to the least destructive button, Tab is trapped, Esc cancels and focus returns to the trigger.
- Toasts are announced as status messages; Undo also has a keyboard path (⌘Z) because toast actions are hard to reach with a keyboard.

## Do

- Do offer Undo after every reversible change, including bulk and assistant changes.
- Do state the consequence in the dialog body.

## Don't

- Don't focus the destructive button by default.

## Related

- Selection and bulk actions
- Propose, then apply
- Notifications: inbox, bell, toast or email digest
- Toast
- Confirmation dialog


---

# Notifications: inbox, bell, toast or email digest

Route every message by one question: does it need this person to act? Things that need you go to the Inbox; your own results go in a toast; nothing gets a separate bell list.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** Products grow a bell, an inbox, toasts, banners and emails that overlap, so people get the same news three times and miss the one that needed them.

**Solution:** The Inbox is the one place for things that need you (agent approvals and questions, listings about to close, mentions, assignments). Toasts only confirm your own actions. Workspace-wide problems use a banner. Email sends a digest of open Inbox items to people who are away.

**Built from:** Inbox (triage), Toast, Banner (inline alert), Notifications vs inbox vs toast, App shell and sidebar navigation, Agent run timeline

## How it works

1. Did this person just do it? Confirm with a toast, or with nothing if the change is already visible.
2. Does it need this person to act or reply? Put it in the Inbox. It stays until marked done (E) or snoozed (⇧H).
3. Does it affect everyone's use of the workspace, such as a broken connection? Show a banner on the affected pages until fixed.
4. Is the person away from TwoUX and is something waiting on them? Send an email digest of open Inbox items, at the frequency they chose.
5. Needs nothing from anyone? Record it in the record's activity only.

## When to use

- Whenever a feature wants to tell someone something. Pick the channel with the steps above before designing the message.

## When not to use

- For validation of what someone typed. Use field messages from Inline editing and validation.
- For errors that need a retry. A toast disappears and cannot hold Retry reliably; use a banner or the error state.

## Guidelines

- No separate bell list. The Inbox count is the only unread count; when the sidebar is hidden, a small inbox button with the same count replaces it.
- Toasts never carry critical warnings or errors and never auto-dismiss something the person must act on.
- Don't resend notifications people have not acted on; let them set email frequency and channels.
- Trivial updates go nowhere but activity. Notification fatigue makes people ignore the important ones.

## Content

- Toasts are past tense and short: "Listing published". Three lines at most.
- Banners say what is affected and what to do: "Workable is disconnected. Reconnect to keep importing candidates."

## Accessibility

- Toasts and count changes are announced as status messages.
- Toasts must not cover the focused element; they appear in an empty corner.
- Anything shown only in a vanishing toast must also be findable elsewhere, such as activity or the Inbox.

## Do

- Do send everything that needs action to the Inbox.
- Do give people control over email frequency.

## Don't

- Don't add a bell next to the Inbox.
- Don't use a toast for errors that need a follow-up.

## Related

- Agents acting on your behalf
- Undo and destructive actions
- Empty, loading and error states
- Inbox (triage)
- Toast
- Banner (inline alert)


---

# Record detail: side panel, overlay or full page

Open a record in a side panel that pushes the list by default, overlay it on narrow or wide-content pages, and go to the full page for deep work.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** Opening records in modals hides the list people compare against; opening a full page every time loses their place. Teams pick a different container on every screen.

**Solution:** Enter or a click opens the side panel in push mode. J and K move to the next record and the panel follows. Esc closes. Open (⇧↵) goes to the full page. Overlay replaces push below about 1100px or when the content needs width.

**Built from:** Side panel (drawer), List table, Data grid, Page header, Breadcrumb, Tabs (underline)

## How it works

1. Enter or a click on a row opens the side panel. The row stays highlighted and the list stays usable.
2. The panel has a control bar (previous, next, position, open full page, close), then ID, title and status, then tabs and sections.
3. J and K move to the next or previous row; the panel follows without closing.
4. Open (⇧↵) moves to the full record page, with breadcrumbs back to the list and the same filters.
5. Esc closes the panel and returns focus to the row that opened it.

## When to use

- Push side panel: on list pages people work through one record after another (listings, candidates, inbox).
- Overlay side panel: when the page is narrower than about 1100px, or holds wide tables or dashboards that pushing would crush.
- Full page: for long records, history, or editing many related sections.

## When not to use

- Don't use a modal dialog for record detail; it hides the rows people compare against. Modals are for confirmations.
- Don't open the detail inline as an expanding row; expanded rows pile up and clutter the table.

## Guidelines

- A split view never replaces the full page; the panel is for deciding the next step, the page is for everything about one record.
- Only one secondary panel of a kind at a time; the assistant and record detail share the same side panel slot.
- Keep the identifying columns visible next to a pushed panel so people know which row they are on.
- People can switch push and overlay with ⇧P, and the choice is remembered.
- With several rows selected, the panel shows a useful summary of the selection, not a list of names.
- The side panel shares the single right-hand slot with the assistant and help panels; opening one replaces the other, and closing it restores the previous one.
- If a form in the panel has unsaved changes, J, K, Esc and close ask before discarding (see Unsaved changes). Single-field edits save on Enter and never ask.
- Section actions sit in each section's header on the right ("Edit details"); record-wide actions sit in the panel footer.
- The Details section shows absolute timestamps with their source: "Created 6 November 2026, 09:14 GMT by Priya Shah".

## Content

- Empty fields say "Add", so the gap is also the way to fill it.
- Timestamps are relative with the exact date on hover.
- Fields the person can't edit are shown as read-only text with the reason on hover, such as "Set by the job board feed".

## Accessibility

- A push panel is non-modal: it sits in the focus order after the list and never traps focus.
- An overlay panel that covers content behaves as a modal dialog: focus moves in, Tab is trapped, Esc closes and focus returns.
- The panel must not fully hide the focused row.

## Do

- Do keep J/K working while the panel is open.
- Do return focus to the row on close.

## Don't

- Don't open record detail in a centred modal.
- Don't open a second panel on top of the first.

## Related

- Keyboard-first navigation
- Inline editing and validation
- Ask about what's on screen
- Side panel (drawer)


---

# Keyboard-first navigation

Every action has a key shown on its button. J/K move, Enter opens, Esc steps back one layer at a time, ⌘K runs anything, ⌘J asks the assistant.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** Power users triage hundreds of rows a day. If shortcuts differ per screen, or Esc sometimes closes a panel and sometimes clears a selection, people stop trusting the keyboard.

**Solution:** One keyboard model across TwoUX: the same keys mean the same thing everywhere, shortcuts are shown on buttons, ? opens the full list, and single-key shortcuts can be turned off.

**Built from:** Command palette (⌘K), Shortcut sheet (?), Keyboard shortcut hint, List table, Side panel (drawer), Assistant side panel, Inbox (triage)

## How it works

1. J and K move the row focus; X selects; ⇧J extends the selection.
2. Enter opens the focused row in the side panel; ⇧↵ opens the full page.
3. Esc closes the top-most layer only, in this order: open menu or popover, then text field edit, then dialog, then side panel, then selection.
4. ⌘K opens the command palette: actions on the current selection first, then Go to. ↑↓ move, ↵ runs, Tab changes scope.
5. ⌘J opens the assistant with the current selection and filters as context.
6. ? opens the shortcut sheet, which also holds the switch for single-key shortcuts.

## When to use

- On every screen. A new action is not finished until it has a key, a place in ⌘K and a hint on its button.

## When not to use

- Don't add single-key shortcuts inside text fields or the composer; there the keys type text.
- Don't make a shortcut the only path to an action; every action is also a visible control.

## Guidelines

- Show the shortcut on the button or menu item itself so people learn it by using the product.
- Keep the set small and mnemonic: C create, E edit, F filter, T extend, D duplicate.
- Avoid ⌘ plus a single key that the browser or OS owns, except deliberate, well-used ones such as ⌘K.
- Single-key shortcuts can be turned off; ⌘ shortcuts stay on.
- Focus is always visible and never lost to the page body when a row or panel disappears.
- Use the same keys as tools people already know (J/K, ⌘K) instead of inventing new ones.

## Content

- Hints use symbols: ⌘K, ⇧↵, Esc. Shown in a muted key cap after the label.
- The shortcut sheet groups keys by Navigate, Table and Act.

## Accessibility

- Everything works by keyboard alone.
- Lists use roving tabindex so Tab enters and leaves a list in one step and arrows move inside it.
- Single-character shortcuts can be turned off for screen reader and voice control users.
- Closing a layer returns focus to the element that opened it.

## Do

- Do keep Esc's order the same on every screen.
- Do list every shortcut in ? and in ⌘K.

## Don't

- Don't let one Esc press close two layers.
- Don't reuse a key for different actions on different pages.

## Related

- Record detail: side panel, overlay or full page
- Selection and bulk actions
- Ask about what's on screen
- Command palette (⌘K)
- Shortcut sheet (?)


---

# Data export

One Export menu on every table: choose what to include first, then the format, then copy instead of download if you want.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** People export to share with hiring managers or to work in a spreadsheet. When each table exports differently, they get files with hidden columns, raw field names or AI guesses mixed with real data.

**Solution:** Export (⇧E) opens one menu: options first (visible columns only, include AI columns, selected rows or all matching rows), then formats, then copy to clipboard. The file matches what is on screen.

**Built from:** Export menu, List table, Data grid, Bulk action bar, Toast, Inbox (triage)

## How it works

1. Export sits in the table toolbar with the other global table actions, and in the bulk bar when rows are selected.
2. Options come first: rows (selected, or all N matching the filters), visible columns only, include AI columns.
3. Then the format (CSV, Excel), then Copy to clipboard for quick pastes.
4. Small exports download at once with a toast. Exports likely to take more than about ten seconds run in the background with progress, and finish with an Inbox item linking to the file.
5. If the export fails, say why and offer Try again in a banner, not a toast.

## When to use

- On any list table, data grid, breakdown table or chart that has a table view.

## When not to use

- To share a view with a colleague inside TwoUX. Share the view's link instead (Saved views).
- As a fix for missing analysis. If many people export the same table, add the analysis to the product.

## Guidelines

- The file matches the screen: same rows, same visible columns, same order, column names as shown, not database field names.
- AI columns are excluded by default and, when included, are named with a suffix such as "(AI)" so generated values are never mistaken for real data.
- Say the scope in numbers before export: "Export 412 candidates".
- Long exports do not block the page; people can keep working.

## Content

- Menu label: "Export". Actions name the scope: "Export 2 rows as CSV".

## Accessibility

- Announce "Export ready" or "Export failed" as a status message.
- The export menu is a standard menu button reachable by keyboard; ⇧E opens it.

## Do

- Do export what the person sees.
- Do label AI columns in the file.

## Don't

- Don't put Export in a different place on each table.
- Don't block the screen while a large export runs.

## Related

- Selection and bulk actions
- Generated table columns and enrichment
- Notifications: inbox, bell, toast or email digest
- Export menu


---

# Comparison over time

Every headline number says what it compares against: this period vs the previous period of the same length, with arrow, sign and colour.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** "312 applications" means nothing on its own. Teams add comparisons in different ways (vs last month, vs last year, percentage or absolute), so numbers on different screens can't be read together.

**Solution:** TwoUX compares the current period with the previous period of the same length by default. Stats show the number, then the change with arrow, sign and colour, then what it is compared with. Charts draw the previous period as a dashed grey line behind the current one.

**Built from:** Stat card with comparison, Line chart card, Breakdown table, Bar chart, Segmented control, Data visualisation colours

## How it works

1. Pick the period with one control above the chart: 7d, 30d, 90d. It drives every chart and stat on the page.
2. The stat leads with the number, then the change ("↑ 18%"), then the comparison in words ("vs 264 the 30 days before").
3. The line chart shows the previous period as a dashed grey line behind the current period, with a legend naming both.
4. Under the chart, the breakdown table shows current and previous side by side and the change in both units.
5. Every chart can switch to a table, which is also its accessible version.

## When to use

- For any KPI or trend on a dashboard, report or record header.
- Next to a single figure in a record, compare with the board median instead of time, so people can judge it without opening a report.

## When not to use

- When there is no previous period (new listing, new team). Show a dash, not "+100%".
- To compare categories in one period. Use a bar chart or breakdown, not a time comparison.

## Guidelines

- Never rely on colour alone for up or down; always add an arrow and a sign.
- Green and red follow meaning, not direction. A fall in time to first apply is good.
- Bars start at zero. Line charts may start elsewhere, but say so on the axis.
- One y-axis per chart. Two measures with different scales get two charts side by side.
- Keep each series the same colour on every chart; status colours never colour a series.
- The current, incomplete period is marked as incomplete so a half week does not look like a drop.

## Content

- Change text: "↑ 18% vs 264 the 30 days before". Units are always stated.
- Chart footer names the source and when it updated: "updated 12 min ago".

## Accessibility

- The change is read as text ("up 18 percent"), not only drawn as an arrow.
- Chart points are reachable with the arrow keys, and the table view carries every number.

## Do

- Do say what every number is compared against.
- Do use the previous period of the same length.

## Don't

- Don't use two y-axes.
- Don't show a percentage change from zero.

## Related

- Data export
- Filtering and search
- Stat card with comparison
- Line chart card
- Breakdown table

# Onboarding to an empty workspace

A new workspace shows a short setup checklist in the sidebar and empty states that each offer one way in: create, import or start from a template.

Kind: pattern · Group: Patterns: general

**Problem:** A new team lands on empty tables and a blank assistant. Product tours get skipped and forgotten, and each feature invents its own first-run screen.

**Solution:** "Get set up 3 / 5" sits in the sidebar until done or dismissed. Each empty page explains what goes there and offers the fastest way in. Templates open as drafts, never run on their own.

**Built from:** App shell and sidebar navigation, Empty state, Templates gallery, Connected tools, Assistant side panel, Button, Setup checklist, Onboarding step

## How it works

1. Show a setup checklist in the sidebar with a count ("Get set up 3 / 5") and the next step underneath.
2. Each step is an action people need anyway: connect your careers page, invite the team, create a first listing, set team instructions, try a saved task.
3. Steps complete themselves when the thing is done anywhere in the product.
4. Each empty page explains what will appear and offers one primary way in, with import or a template as the second.
5. Templates open as an editable draft that names the tools it uses. Nothing runs until the person chooses Run.
6. The checklist can be dismissed and reopened from Settings.

## When to use

- For a new workspace, and for a feature someone opens for the first time (a blank slate).

## When not to use

- Don't open a product tour or deck of cards on first login; show help when people reach the feature.
- For a list that is empty because of filters. Use the zero results state.

## Guidelines

- Keep the checklist to five steps or fewer, ordered by value to the team.
- Offer starter content (sample listings) only if it is clearly marked and easy to remove; keep a plain empty state for when it is gone.
- Show help in context and on request, not up front.
- The assistant's empty state offers two or three tasks based on what is on screen, not a blank "How can I help?".
- Say early what the assistant can and can't do with the workspace's data.
- Track checklist steps as tasks done or not done, not progress inside a task. A step left halfway still shows as not done.
- Recommend a setting when it helps, but never stop people choosing another one. Warn only when their choice blocks the goal of the step.
- Show steps that can't start yet and say what they need first, such as "Connect your careers page first". Don't hide them.
- Support both people who read first and people who try first: a short line and Learn more on each step, and an action that starts the task straight away.
- Once the checklist is dismissed it stays dismissed on every page until reopened from Settings.

## Content

- Blank slate titles invite the action: "Create your first listing". Body says why in one sentence.
- Checklist steps start with a verb and say the benefit: "Connect your careers page to import roles automatically".

## Accessibility

- The checklist progress is text ("3 of 5 done"), not only a ring.
- Completing a step is announced as a status message.
- Recommendation popovers attached to a step open one at a time, never on their own, and close with Esc.

## Do

- Do show progress through setup.
- Do give every empty page a way in.

## Don't

- Don't block the product behind a setup wizard.
- Don't run a template without the person choosing Run.

## Related

- Empty, loading and error states
- Saved tasks and schedules
- Ask about what's on screen
- Empty state
- Templates gallery
- Onboarding step
- Setup checklist
- Sign in
